pos: n. (the name Rachel gave her second son as she died; changed by Jacob to Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Ben-oni, the son of my sorrow, from ben, a son, and oni, sorrow or affliction; named once, Genesis 35:18.
biblical_def: Benoni is a name spoken once, by a dying woman, and immediately overruled by her husband: “And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin” (Genesis 35:18). The Authorized Version's margin gives both meanings — the son of my sorrow, and the son of the right hand. The setting is given in the verses around it: “And they journeyed from Bethel; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour” (Genesis 35:16), and then “And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem” (Genesis 35:19). Rachel named the child out of what was happening to her; Jacob named him out of what the child would be to the family. Both namings are true, and Scripture records both without resolving the tension by deleting one. The place of her death is noted because it matters later: it is Bethlehem, where another mother's son would be born, and where the weeping of Rachel would be heard again.

webster_full: Hebrew Ben-oni, the son of my sorrow.

corruption_summary: Grief is treated as a stage to be processed and left behind; Scripture lets a mother name her sorrow truly and a father name the promise truly, and keeps both on the page.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic language around bereavement works toward resolution: the feeling is named in order to be moved through, and a name like son of my sorrow would be counted unhealthy, a wound carried into the next generation. Genesis 35 does not treat Rachel's word as a pathology. It records what she said, records that she died saying it, and records that her husband gave the boy a different name to live under. The grief is not denied, minimised, or processed. It is simply true, and so is the hope that overrules it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is near to the grieving without requiring them to pretend: “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit” (Psalm 34:18). Rachel died on the road to Bethlehem, and the tribe her son fathered gave Israel its first king and the apostle to the Gentiles. A name born of sorrow became a name of the right hand, which is the pattern the whole of Scripture follows.

pos: n. (the son of Lot by his younger daughter, father of the Ammonites)
etymology: Hebrew Ben-ammi, the son of my people, or son of my kindred, from ben, a son, and am, a people; named once, Genesis 19:38.
biblical_def: Benammi is named once, at the end of the worst scene in Lot's life: “And the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Benammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day” (Genesis 19:38). The sentence before it states the sin without euphemism: “Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father” (Genesis 19:36), and the circumstance is given plainly as well: “And Lot went up out of Zoar, and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he feared to dwell in Zoar: and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters” (Genesis 19:30). The name means son of my people — a claim of kinship made by a woman who had just destroyed the ordinary meaning of kinship. From that son came a nation that warred against Israel for a thousand years, and the law set a term on its standing: “An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation shall they not enter into the congregation of the LORD for ever” (Deuteronomy 23:3). Scripture tells the whole story, including the part that reflects badly on the man it elsewhere calls righteous.

corruption_summary: Scripture is accused of endorsing what it narrates; Genesis 19 reports incest plainly, names the nation that came of it, and never once commends the act.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge that the Bible approves of the atrocities it records runs onto this chapter and breaks. Genesis 19 gives the reader an unflinching account — the daughters contrive it, the father is made drunk, two sons are born — with no softening and no commendation. The narrative voice simply says what happened and then follows the consequence for a thousand years of national history. That is the difference between a text that reports sin and a text that sanctions it, and the distinction is not difficult once a reader is willing to make it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of Scripture about its own people. Lot is called righteous in the New Testament and is shown here at his lowest; Abraham, Jacob, David and Peter are all handled the same way. A book written to flatter its heroes would have ended Lot's story at Zoar. And the mercy at the far end is remarkable: the law barred Ammon and Moab, and Ruth the Moabitess still came into the congregation by faith, and into the line of Christ.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Kish, and so of Saul, in the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Bekorath, firstborn, or the firstborn, from bekor, a firstborn son; named once, 1 Samuel 9:1.
biblical_def: Bechorath appears in the one verse that gives Saul's descent: “Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power” (1 Samuel 9:1). His name means firstborn, and he stands four generations above a young man introduced in the next verse: “And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2). Saul's own estimate of his house was the opposite of what his ancestor's name suggests: “Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?” (1 Samuel 9:21). The choice was nevertheless made publicly and by lot: “When he had caused the tribe of Benjamin to come near by their families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was taken: and when they sought him, he could not be found” (1 Samuel 10:21). A man called Firstborn stands in the ancestry of Israel's first king.

corruption_summary: Primogeniture is dismissed as arbitrary privilege; in Scripture the firstborn is an office with a double portion and a duty, and one God repeatedly reassigns by grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern reading treats the rights of the firstborn as mere accident of birth order weaponised into privilege, and finds the whole institution offensive. Scripture is both more structured and more subversive than that. The firstborn held a real office — a double portion, the headship of the house, the priestly duty toward the family — and God overturned it again and again by His own choice: Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah and Joseph over Reuben, David the eighth son over seven elder brothers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that standing before God is never inherited. A man named Firstborn fathered the house of Israel's first king, and that king was chosen out of the tribe he himself called the smallest of the tribes of Israel, from the family he called the least. The kingdom was given, not owed, and when Saul forfeited it, it passed to a shepherd. The true Firstborn, in whom the office is finally lodged, came of Judah.

pos: n. (the earliest named ancestor of Saul, in the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Aphiach, I will make to breathe, or refreshed, from a root meaning to breathe or blow; named once, 1 Samuel 9:1.
biblical_def: Aphiah is the furthest back Scripture traces the house of Saul: “Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power” (1 Samuel 9:1). Five names, ending in his, and then the narrative moves straight to the son who would be king: “And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2). The genealogy exists to answer a question the nation would ask about a king chosen from the smallest tribe. When the choice was made by lot the family had to be identified in public: “When he had caused the tribe of Benjamin to come near by their families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was taken: and when they sought him, he could not be found” (1 Samuel 10:21). Saul's own words about his house are on record: “and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin?” (1 Samuel 9:21). Aphiah is the head of that least family.

corruption_summary: Leadership is assumed to arise from the strongest quarter; Israel's first king came from the smallest tribe and, by his own account, from its least family.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of every age is that power should come from where power already is, and the narrative of Saul's election is built to frustrate that instinct. Benjamin had been nearly annihilated in the days of the judges; it was the smallest tribe, and Saul names his own clan the least within it. Yet the lot fell there, in public, before the whole nation, and the man had to be fetched from where he was hiding among the baggage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's choices do not follow strength, and that He takes no counsel from the obvious. Aphiah is named for breath, and his house was the thinnest reed in Israel; the kingdom was set upon it anyway. What Saul did with it afterward is the warning half of the story, but the election itself displays a God who deliberately chooses the small, so that no flesh may glory in His presence.

pos: n. (a son of Ezer, a Horite chief of the land of Seir; written Jakan in Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Aqan, sharp-sighted, or twisted, of uncertain derivation; named once in this form, Genesis 36:27, and as Jakan at 1 Chronicles 1:42.
biblical_def: Akan is named once in Genesis, in the register of the people who held Edom before Israel existed: “The children of Ezer are these; Bilhan, and Zaavan, and Akan” (Genesis 36:27). The Chronicler gives the same list with the name in its other form: “The sons of Ezer; Bilhan, and Zavan, and Jakan. The sons of Dishan; Uz, and Aran” (1 Chronicles 1:42), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two spellings as one name. The people he belongs to are introduced by their father: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah” (Genesis 36:20). Moses then records something that has to be read twice to be believed: “And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel” (Genesis 36:31). Scripture keeps the genealogy of a dispossessed Gentile people, and keeps the roll of their kings, and says frankly that they had kingship before Israel did. Akan is one name in that record.

corruption_summary: Scripture is charged with erasing the peoples Israel displaced; Genesis 36 preserves the Horite genealogy and the Edomite king list in detail, before Israel had a king at all.
corruption_paragraphs: A standard criticism holds that the Hebrew Scriptures write conquered peoples out of history. Genesis 36 is a chapter-length refutation. It gives the sons of Seir the Horite by name, the chiefs of Edom, the sons of each chief, the kings who reigned in Edom, and the cities they reigned from — and it states that this kingship preceded Israel's. No triumphal note is struck anywhere in it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God of Scripture is the God of the nations and keeps account of them all. Edom was Israel's brother and became its bitter enemy, and the prophets pronounced judgment on it; that judgment presupposes the record, not its erasure. A dictionary that keeps Akan keeps faith with a text that troubled itself to write down the sons of men whose land its readers would inherit.

pos: n. (a son of Gad, head of the family of the Arodites; written Arodi in Genesis)
etymology: Hebrew Arod, a wild ass, or one who roams, from a root meaning to roam or flee; named once in this form, Numbers 26:17, and as Arodi at Genesis 46:16.
biblical_def: Arod is one of the seven sons of Gad, and the head of a family counted in the wilderness census: “Of Arod, the family of the Arodites: of Areli, the family of the Arelites” (Numbers 26:17). The earlier list, taken when Jacob's house went down into Egypt, spells the name Arodi: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16), and the Authorized Version's margin notes the two as one man. The census closes with the tribe's strength: “These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). Gad took its inheritance east of Jordan and lived where the raiding came from, which is why Moses blessed it as he did: “And of Gad he said, Blessed be he that enlargeth Gad: he dwelleth as a lion, and teareth the arm with the crown of the head” (Deuteronomy 33:20). A family named for the wild ass of the desert settled on the desert's edge and held it.

corruption_summary: Variant spellings across the censuses are treated as evidence of rival documents; the Authorized Version's own margin treats them as one man recorded twice.
corruption_paragraphs: The two Gadite lists differ in several names, and the documentary approach assigns them to separate sources centuries apart, so that Arod and Arodi become traces of competing traditions rather than one man. The simpler account is the one the text itself supplies: the lists were taken more than two hundred years apart, in different languages of administration, and a name that ends in a gentilic suffix in one register appears bare in the other. The margin of the Authorized Version said so plainly in 1611.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the continuity of the covenant people through the generations in Egypt. Seven sons went down with Jacob; seven families came out and were numbered at forty thousand five hundred. That is not the record of a nation inventing its past but of a nation counting what God had multiplied, exactly as He had promised Abraham.

pos: n. (a son of Gilead, head of the family of the Helekites, of the tribe of Manasseh)
etymology: Hebrew Cheleq, a portion, or a share, from chalaq, to divide or apportion; named twice, Numbers 26:30 and Joshua 17:2.
biblical_def: Helek's name means a portion, and both times Scripture mentions him it is in the act of apportioning land. He is counted among the families of Manasseh in the wilderness: “These are the sons of Gilead: of Jeezer, the family of the Jeezerites: of Helek, the family of the Helekites” (Numbers 26:30), under the house named just before: “Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29). Then he is named again at the division of Canaan: “There was also a lot for the rest of the children of Manasseh by their families; for the children of Abiezer, and for the children of Helek, and for the children of Asriel, and for the children of Shechem, and for the children of Hepher, and for the children of Shemida: these were the male children of Manasseh the son of Joseph by their families” (Joshua 17:2). The very next verse records the famous exception among his kinsmen: “But Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, had no sons, but daughters” (Joshua 17:3), and those daughters received a portion too.

corruption_summary: The allotment of Canaan is read as the charter of a land seizure; Scripture presents it as an inheritance distributed by lot, by family, with provision made even for daughters without brothers.
corruption_paragraphs: The conquest is the hardest ground in the Old Testament for a modern conscience, and the allotment chapters are often read as the paperwork of dispossession. What the chapters actually describe is a distribution the recipients did not control: the land was assigned by lot, so no family could bargain for a better portion, and the measure was household by household. The nations displaced had filled the measure of their iniquity over four hundred years of divine patience, and Israel was warned it would be vomited out in turn for the same sins. It was.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an inheritance is received and not seized — which is the force of Helek's own name. The provision for Zelophehad's daughters, recorded in the verse immediately after his, shows the system bending to protect those with no claim under its ordinary rules. God apportions, and He does it justly, including to the ones the rules would have left out.

pos: n. (a son of Benjamin, head of the family of the Huphamites)
etymology: Hebrew Chupham, coast-man, or protected, of uncertain derivation; named once, Numbers 26:39, and read in the margin as Huppim at Genesis 46:21.
biblical_def: Hupham heads one of the Benjamite families counted on the plains of Moab: “Of Shupham, the family of the Shuphamites: of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites” (Numbers 26:39). The earliest Benjamite list gives the name in another form: “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21), where the Authorized Version's margin notes Huppim as Hupham and Muppim as Shupham. The census closes with the tribe's number: “These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred” (Numbers 26:41). That figure is worth holding beside what came later, for Benjamin was reduced to six hundred men in the civil war of the judges and had to be rebuilt from them. The register in Numbers counts a tribe at full strength, listing families by name — “of Ahiram, the family of the Ahiramites” (Numbers 26:38) among them — before the near-extinction and the slow recovery.

corruption_summary: Tribal censuses are dismissed as literary invention; they are the baseline against which Scripture itself records Benjamin's near-destruction and recovery.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers is routinely treated as late priestly bookkeeping, its figures symbolic rather than counted. But the numbers do work in the narrative that follows. Benjamin is counted here at forty-five thousand six hundred; in the book of Judges the tribe is cut down to six hundred men hiding at the rock Rimmon; in Chronicles its registers are patchy and its lists differ, exactly as the records of a reconstituted tribe would. The census is the premise of the later story, not an ornament on it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God numbers His people and then preserves a remnant of them through judgments they bring on themselves. Benjamin's sin at Gibeah was as foul as Sodom's, and the tribe nearly ceased to exist for it. From its six hundred survivors came Saul, and Mordecai, and Paul. A family name like Hupham's survives on the far side of that, which is mercy written in a census.

pos: n. (a son of Shobal the father of Kirjath-jearim, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Haroeh, the seer, or the one who sees, from raah, to see, with the article prefixed; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:52, and read in the margin as Reaiah.
biblical_def: Haroeh is named once: “And Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim had sons; Haroeh, and half of the Manahethites” (1 Chronicles 2:52). The name keeps the Hebrew article and means the seer, the same word used of Samuel and of the prophets who advised the kings; the Authorized Version's margin offers Reaiah as the reading. His father's standing is given just above: “These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim” (1 Chronicles 2:50). The verses that follow set out the clans that came of this house: “And the families of Kirjathjearim; the Ithrites, and the Puhites, and the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; of them came the Zareathites, and the Eshtaulites” (1 Chronicles 2:53), and then the parallel branch: “The sons of Salma; Bethlehem, and the Netophathites, Ataroth, the house of Joab, and half of the Manahethites, the Zorites” (1 Chronicles 2:54). Kirjath-jearim is where the ark rested for twenty years after the Philistines sent it back, and Bethlehem stands in the same paragraph. Haroeh belongs to the house that held both towns.

corruption_summary: Seeing is now the credential of the visionary who speaks for himself; in Scripture the seer is a man who reports what he was shown, and is judged by whether it was true.
corruption_paragraphs: The title seer has been absorbed into a religious market of visions and personal revelations, where the claim to have seen is its own authority and no one is permitted to test it. Scripture ties the office to verification from the start: a seer who says what does not come to pass is no prophet, and the canon is closed. The continuing claims of modern apostles and prophets fall under that same test and fail it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the importance of the places the registers quietly name. Shobal's house held Kirjath-jearim, where the ark lodged twenty years while Israel lamented after the LORD, and the next verse names Bethlehem. The Chronicler is tracing the towns of Judah through the families that held them, and the two towns that mattered most in the history of the ark and of the Christ are a verse apart in the list.

pos: n. (the firstborn son of Nahor, Abraham's brother)
etymology: Hebrew Uts, wooded, or counsel, the same name elsewhere rendered Uz; named once in this form, Genesis 22:21.
biblical_def: Huz is named once, as the eldest of eight sons born to Abraham's brother: “Huz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram” (Genesis 22:21). The news of the family reaches Abraham just after the binding of Isaac: “And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor” (Genesis 22:20), and the list closes with the name that matters to the narrative: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Genesis 22:23). The marriages of the two brothers are recorded earlier: “And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah” (Genesis 11:29). The whole point of the eight names is the last one. Isaac has just been given back to Abraham from the altar, and the next thing the reader is told is that a girl has been born in Mesopotamia who will become his wife. Huz heads a list whose purpose is Rebekah.

corruption_summary: Genealogies are read as interruptions to the story; this one is placed immediately after the binding of Isaac because it carries the answer to what Isaac will need next.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader trained on narrative tension treats Genesis 22:20-24 as an appendix tacked onto the end of a great chapter, and skips it. The placement is deliberate and the effect is considerable. Abraham has just received his son back from the altar, with the promise of a seed through him reaffirmed in the strongest terms God ever used. The next paragraph reports that eight children have been born to his brother in Mesopotamia, and names a granddaughter: Rebekah. Two chapters later a servant travels there to find her.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence works through family news nobody recognises as providence at the time. Huz was the firstborn and is named first; the line of promise ran through his youngest brother's daughter. God had the wife ready before the son was spared, and told Abraham about it in a list of names he had no way of reading as a promise.
